Empirical Research Plan: Differential Treatment of Job Applicants by Perceived Race  

-------------------------------------------------------------

1. Identification Strategy  
Method: Randomized field experiment (correspondence audit).  
Rationale:  
• Resumes are created by the researcher and randomly assigned either an African-American‐identifying name or a White-identifying name before they are sent to the same pool of employers.  
• Because treatment is randomly assigned ex-ante, treated and control resumes are, in expectation, identical on all observed and unobserved characteristics except for the racial signal.  
• Causal effects are therefore obtained by comparing callback rates between the two groups; no difference-in-differences, IV, or RDD is necessary.  
• We can still use regression to improve precision and to study heterogeneous effects (e.g., interaction with resume quality), but identification ultimately rests on the randomized assignment.

2. Treatment and Control  
Treatment variable:  
  T_i = 1 if resume i carries a distinctly African-American first name (e.g., “Latonya,” “Jamal”);  
  T_i = 0 if resume i carries a distinctly White first name (e.g., “Emily,” “Greg”).  

Control group: resumes with White-identifying names.  

Treatment timing: instantaneous at the moment the resume is sent; there is no staggered adoption or event date beyond that.  

Additional (orthogonal) experimental arm: high-quality versus low-quality resumes (Q_i = 1 for high quality). This allows testing whether higher credentials reduce the racial gap (interaction term T_i × Q_i).

3. Key Identifying Assumptions  
A1. Random Assignment: Names (race signal) and quality are assigned independently of all resume content other than the manipulated characteristics.  
• Plausibility: Assignment is under the researcher’s control; implementation logs can verify randomization.

A2. Stable Unit Treatment Value (SUTVA): The treatment status of one resume does not affect the callback probability of another.  
• Plausibility: Employers are unlikely to link multiple fictitious resumes to the same applicant because each has a unique name, phone number, and e-mail. Some risk remains if an employer spots duplicates within the same ad, but that can be mitigated by sending at most two resumes per ad and varying addresses and contact details.

A3. No Differential Measurement Error: Callback measurement is equally accurate for both racial signals.  
• Plausibility: All resumes use voice-mail boxes and dedicated e-mail addresses that automatically record contacts, independent of race signal.

A4. No Differential Attrition: All resumes remain in the experiment; there is no attrition once they are sent.

A5. Correct Model Specification (for regression, not for identification): If we use a linear probability model (LPM) with fixed effects, we must cluster standard errors at the ad level.

4. Threats to Identification and Mitigation  

Threat 1: Implementation or coding errors break randomization.  
 • Check and Document: Conduct balance tests on observable characteristics.  
 • Fix: If imbalance appears, include those characteristics as controls and document that results are robust.

Threat 2: Within-ad interference (employer realizes two resumes are fictitious or linked).  
 • Design: Limit to ≤ 2 resumes per ad and space their fax/e-mail submissions.  
 • Robustness: Re-estimate dropping ads that received more than one experimental resume.

Threat 3: Names may convey socioeconomic cues in addition to race.  
 • Mitigation:  
  – Show that observable resume content (education, address, work history) is balanced across name types.  
  – Use Census zip-code controls for neighborhood income/education to partial out any socioeconomic inference.  
  – Report that results are robust to including mother’s education-based “social class” name scores.

5. R Code Outline  

```r
# Install/load packages
install.packages(c("data.table", "fixest", "sandwich", "lmtest"))
library(data.table); library(fixest); library(sandwich); library(lmtest)

# 1. Load data  --------------------------------------------------------------
res <- fread("resumes.csv")          # One row = one resume
ads  <- fread("ads.csv")             # Ad-level info (optional)

# 2. Merge and basic variable creation --------------------------------------
res <- merge(res, ads, by = "ad_id", all.x = TRUE)

# Treatment indicator
res[, black := ifelse(race_signal == "Black", 1, 0)]

# Resume quality indicator already coded as 'high_quality' (1/0)
# Outcome: callback (1 = phone or e-mail invitation, 0 otherwise)

# 3. Main specification ------------------------------------------------------
# Linear probability model with ad fixed effects, city × occupation FEs
main_mod <- feols(callback ~ black + high_quality + black:high_quality | ad_id + city*occupation,
                  data = res, cluster = "ad_id")

summary(main_mod)

# 4. Robustness checks -------------------------------------------------------
# (i) Logistic regression without FEs
logit_mod <- feglm(callback ~ black + high_quality + black:high_quality + city + occupation,
                   data = res, family = binomial("logit"), cluster = "ad_id")
summary(logit_mod)

# (ii) Drop ads with two experimental resumes
single_res <- res[, .N, by = ad_id][N == 1][, ad_id]
main_mod_single <- feols(callback ~ black + high_quality + black:high_quality | city*occupation,
                         data = res[ad_id %in% single_res], cluster = "ad_id")
summary(main_mod_single)

# (iii) Include zip-code socioeconomic controls
soc_mod <- feols(callback ~ black + high_quality + black:high_quality +
                 zip_unemp + zip_medinc + zip_pct_black | ad_id + city*occupation,
                 data = res, cluster = "ad_id")
summary(soc_mod)
```

6. Expected Results  
Theory (taste-based or statistical discrimination) and existing audit studies predict fewer callbacks for resumes signaling African-American identity. Prior:  
• Baseline callback rate for White names ≈ 10–12 %.  
• African-American penalty ≈ −3 to −4 percentage points (≈ 25–30 % relative decline).  
• Interaction: High-quality resumes raise callbacks for both groups, but the incremental gain is smaller for Black-signaling resumes, so the racial gap persists (possibly widens slightly).

7. Validity Checklist Self-Assessment (1 = satisfied, 0 = questionable)  
C1: Random assignment properly implemented …………………… 1  
C2: No interference/SUTVA ……………………………………………… 1 (minor concerns but mitigated)  
C3: Outcome measured consistently across arms …………… 1  
C4: Low missing data/attrition ………………………………………… 1  
C5: Balance on observables confirmed …………………………… 1  

Total = 5/5.
